title: Comparative Evolutionary Anthropology (CEA)
text:
We welcome applications from motivated students and researchers who share our interest in the evolution of humans and primates. The lab is based at the School of Anthropology and Museum Ethnography, University of Oxford.
Please read the descriptions below and get in touch with a CV and a brief description of your research interests before making a formal application.


  DPhil (PhD)
  
  
    We supervise DPhil students through the 
    
    DPhil in Anthropology at the University of Oxford. Strong candidates will have a 
    background in biological anthropology, evolutionary biology, zoology, or a related field, 
    and ideally some experience with quantitative or computational methods (morphometrics, 
    phylogenetics, biomechanics, or statistics).
  
  
    Funding is available through Oxford's graduate scholarship schemes and external fellowships 
    (e.g. Clarendon, NERC DTP). We encourage prospective students to contact Thomas 
    well in advance of application deadlines to discuss project ideas.
  



  Postdoctoral
  
  
    We are interested in hosting postdoctoral researchers through fellowship schemes such as:
  
  
    Leverhulme Early Career Fellowship
    Newton International Fellowship (Royal Society)
    Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions
    Wellcome Early Career Award
    HFSP Postdoctoral Fellowship
  
  If you are interested in applying for any of these with Thomas as a sponsor, please get in touch.



  Visiting
  
  
    We welcome visiting researchers and graduate students for short- or medium-term stays. 
    Oxford offers several mechanisms for formal visiting student status. Please contact 
    Thomas to discuss possibilities.
  


Contact: thomas.puschel@anthro.ox.ac.uk
Address: Institute of Human Sciences, The Pauling Centre, 58a Banbury Rd, Oxford OX2 6QS, UK

title: Comparative Evolutionary Anthropology (CEA)
text:
We take a comparative approach to understanding human uniqueness, combining biological anthropology, palaeontology, and evolutionary biology to investigate how and why humans and other primates came to look and behave as they do today. Our work draws on a broad methodological toolkit:


  
    
      🦴
      
      We use geometric morphometrics and 3D scanning to quantify anatomical variation across 
      primates and hominins, identifying patterns of shape change through evolutionary time and 
      testing hypotheses about adaptation and constraint.
    
  

  
    
      ⚙️
      
      We use computational modelling to reconstruct and investigate the biomechanical performance of biological structures and systems in living and extinct species. Combining approaches such as finite element analysis, computational fluid dynamics, and musculoskeletal modelling, we explore locomotion, feeding, tool use, and other functional adaptations throughout human and primate evolution.
    
  

  
    
      🌳
      
      We develop and apply statistical methods for analysing trait evolution along phylogenetic 
      trees — estimating divergence times, modelling rates of morphological and life-history 
      change, and testing macroevolutionary hypotheses across primates and hominins.
    
  

  
    
      🧠
      
      A major focus is on the evolution of encephalization and body size in the hominin lineage — 
      including the timing, tempo, and drivers of brain expansion, and what distinguishes 
      Homo sapiens from earlier hominins and our primate relatives.
    
  

  
    
      🦧
      
      We investigate the adaptive radiation of primates — how they diversified into different 
      ecological niches, how their locomotor and dietary anatomy evolved, and what drives 
      macroevolutionary patterns of diversification and body plan innovation.
    
  

  
    
      🌍
      
      We participate in the 
      Palaeo-Primate Project 
      in Gorongosa National Park, Mozambique, recovering Miocene fossil primates from 
      the southern East African Rift — some of the oldest known from coastal woodland environments.

title: A comparative perspectiveon human uniqueness
text:
What makes us human? We believe that question only makes sense in comparative context.
        By placing our species alongside other species we identify which features of human
        anatomy, behaviour, and evolution are genuinely distinctive, which are shared, and which
        arose repeatedly across the tree of life. Human uniqueness becomes clearer, not weaker,
        when examined through a comparative lens.
      
      
        Our Research

title: Comparative Evolutionary Anthropology (CEA)
text:
Wendy James Associate Professor in Evolutionary Anthropology
      School of Anthropology and Museum Ethnography, University of Oxford
      Tutorial Fellow, St Hugh's College
    
    
      Thomas leads the Comparative Evolutionary Anthropology (CEA) group at the University of Oxford. His research seeks to understand what makes humans unique by placing our species in comparative context — alongside other primates and mammals — and asking which features of human anatomy, behaviour, and evolution are genuinely distinctive, which are shared with our relatives, and which evolved independently across the tree of life. To address these questions he draws on an integrative toolkit spanning 3D morphometrics, virtual computational biomechanics, phylogenetic comparative methods, and fieldwork, applied to both living species and the fossil record.
    
    
      He completed his PhD at the University of Manchester (2018), his MSc at the University of York,
      and his undergraduate degree at the University of Chile. He was a Leverhulme Early Career Fellow
      at Oxford and a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Reading before taking up his
      current position in 2023.
    
    
      ORCID
      Google Scholar
      GitHub
      Twitter/X
      Email
    
  







  
    
      
      
      DPhil Candidate
      Reece is a biological anthropologist interested in primate and hominin life history evolution. His DPhil research uses phylogenetic comparative methods and Bayesian modelling to reconstruct reproductive strategies in extinct hominins, asking how and when distinctively human patterns of interbirth interval, offspring dependency, and cooperative breeding emerged across our evolutionary lineage.
      Research interests: Life history evolution, reproductive biology, hominin evolution, phylogenetic comparative methods, Bayesian statistics
    
  

  
    
      
      
      DPhil Candidate
      Rachel is a biological anthropologist broadly interested in how osteological remains — and specifically the post-crania — can provide insight into modern human and primate adaptations, as well as help reconstruct the lives of our ancestors. Her DPhil research focuses on whether and how lateralized behaviours impact directional asymmetry in bones of the hand across the primate order, with a particular focus on our closest living relatives, the great apes. She has a background in human anatomy, and worked in clinical research at Michigan Medicine for four years before coming to Oxford for her MSc.
      Research interests: Osteology, palaeoanthropology, primatology, laterality, handedness, anatomy, hominin evolution
      MSc Cognitive & Evolutionary Anthropology, University of Oxford (2023) · BS Evolutionary Anthropology, University of Michigan (2018)
      
        ORCID
        BlueSky
      
    
  








  
    
      
      
      Postdoctoral Affiliate · now at University of Oxford (School of Anthropology)
      Gabriele studies how children in harsh and unpredictable environments develop hidden abilities, combining experimental cognitive studies with ethnographic fieldwork in Brazilian favelas, southern Italy, Roma communities, and rural Mozambique. He also examines community-based martial arts programmes as settings for children's wellbeing, working with local NGOs to translate research findings into culturally grounded education and support initiatives.
      DPhil Anthropology, University of Oxford · MSc Cognitive & Evolutionary Anthropology, University of Oxford
      
        Oxford Profile
        Email
      
    
  






We work with researchers at institutions including the University of Reading, the University of Manchester, the Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona, and the University of Chile, as well as colleagues in the Palaeo-Primate Project.
Interested in collaborating? Get in touch.
